facts.claim: "Tennessee" is track 1 on P.S. Eliot's album Introverted Romance In Our Troubled Minds, released June 1, 2009 on Salinas Records. It runs 3:04.
Katie Crutchfield sings lead on "Tennessee". The song comes from the band's first full-length album.

The album credits list Matt Whitson as engineer and producer, with engineering and production help from P.S. Eliot. Credited band members are Allison Crutchfield (drums, vocals), Katie Crutchfield, Katherine Simonetti (bass) and Will Granger (guitar, vocals).
The album's Discogs notes say the songs were recorded in November 2008 at the band's old house in Tuscaloosa, Alabama.
Katie Crutchfield said the album was recorded at the band's Tuscaloosa house in one weekend. The band wanted to record everything live, and the engineer said the LP was mostly recorded in two days.
Songfacts describes "Tennessee" as a love song about romance and escape. Its destination, Tennessee, is about a three-hour drive up I-65 from Birmingham.
A 2016 review of the P.S. Eliot compilation 2007-2011 quotes "Tennessee" as the album opener and cites its line about quitting at twenty-five.

P.S. Eliot formed in Birmingham, Alabama in 2007 and was led by twin sisters Katie (guitar, vocals) and Allison Crutchfield (drums). Their core lineup later added bassist Katherine Simonetti and guitarist Will Granger.

The band's catalog is the Bike Wreck demo (2008), Introverted Romance In Our Troubled Minds (2009), the Living in Squalor EP (2010) and Sadie (2011). Don Giovanni collected it all in the 2016 set 2007-2011.
The band broke up in 2011 after moving to Brooklyn. Katie Crutchfield went on to form Waxahatchee in 2010, following the breakup of P.S. Eliot.

research.lineage: P.S. Eliot sits in the DIY pop-punk and indie-rock scene of Birmingham, Alabama, centered on the Cave 9 venue, and was an explicitly feminist band within a male-dominated punk scene.

draft:
"I've got affection to criticise." That's the first line of the first song on P.S. Eliot's first full-length, and it sets out the whole problem. Before **Tennessee** gets anywhere near a love song, Katie Crutchfield lists her defenses: monogamy to scorn, a cold heart, an altered state of mind. Then the turn comes, almost a punchline: "baby, you're just what I'm looking for." The narrator isn't giving up the armor. They want someone who will wear it with them.

That tension carries the whole song. The narrator brags about feeling indestructible, says they'll quit when they're 25, waves off sleep until death. It's the swagger of being young and broke, and it's real. But the lines keep giving away their own doubt. The narrator calls themself a pessimist. They point out that this other person has made a mess of this road before. Then, in the last section, comes a line that undercuts every boast: a "mental image of the way you used to look at me." "Used to" is the giveaway. Even as the song pushes forward, part of it is already looking back at something that may be slipping. Hope and dread sit side by side, and the song doesn't sort them out.

The escape it offers is small and specific, which is why it lands. Tennessee is roughly three hours up I-65 from Birmingham, where the band started in 2007. The details are road-trip details, sharp and a little ugly: "Butterfly guts on the windshield," smoke trailing out the window. And the plan is only as big as the tank: "I've got a racing mind and enough gas to get to Tennessee." That isn't freedom forever. It's one night's worth, and the triple "tonight" at the close admits as much.

The sound is plain and close. A picked acoustic guitar strums the chords, the bass holds the root notes, and the drums keep a simple kick-snare-hi-hat beat at a relaxed medium tempo with a slight swing. Crutchfield's voice is clear and a little breathy, a single line with no harmonies, melodic but carrying weight. The arrangement holds steady instead of building, which lets the words do the pushing. That directness fits how it was made. The band recorded the album live at their old house in Tuscaloosa in November 2008, mostly over two days, with Matt Whitson engineering. Allison Crutchfield, Katie's twin, plays drums.

P.S. Eliot came out of Birmingham's DIY punk scene around the Cave 9 venue, an openly feminist band in a mostly male world. Katie Crutchfield later went on to Waxahatchee, and the line that runs through both bands is already here: confessional writing that refuses to make the narrator look better than they are. "Tennessee" is pop-punk with the volume turned down and the nerve left in.

It sticks because it captures the exact moment when you know a thing probably won't last, decide to drive toward it anyway, and count the gas instead of the odds.
